text:
From automatic links
to explainable notebook navigation
Functional differentiation · formative study · technical evaluation · user study
Purpose: convert the professor's feedback into a defensible research plan. The proposed contribution remains a hypothesis until the formative study validates the target users and tasks.
What the literature supports — and what it does not
Formative evidence can reveal pain points and turn them into design requirements. InterLink used interviews; Themisto used an in-depth analysis of 80 notebooks.
Overview, zoom, filter, details-on-demand, relate, history and extract are established information-seeking tasks.
History is not automatically a contribution. The novelty must be the specific history behavior, target task and measured benefit.

Your reasoning is aligned. Reframe “history” as a testable design hypothesis: a semantic trail of visited relationships that helps readers resume, revisit and compare evidence across code, Markdown and outputs.
The defensible gap relative to InterLink
Shows exact evidence, reason and provenance
Uses manually reviewed link sets in evaluation
Measures link quality against expert annotations
Tests code-first progressive disclosure and semantic history
Automatic, inspectable relationship creation + navigation designed around evidence verification.

InterLink states that relationship specification is future work and studies the presentation of specified links. For its evaluation, two formative-study participants annotated relationships and reviewed/refined them with the authors. Source: https://arxiv.org/html/2502.16114
Create multi-granular Markdown–code–output candidates; use output text and generating code as evidence.
Expose exact spans, localized chart/table regions, confidence and a human-readable reason.
Code-first overview, on-demand related text, focus mode and a trail for resuming prior relationship visits.
The value is not “more links”; it is faster and more accurate verification of why notebook elements belong together.
The three parts should not be claimed as validated contributions yet. The formative study and staged evaluations establish which parts solve real tasks and which should be removed or revised.
Formative study: turn assumptions into requirements

6–10 practicing data scientists
with shared-notebook experience
Walk through a recent unfamiliar notebook; think aloud and identify breakdowns
Critical incidents: finding evidence, revisiting results, checking outputs, trusting links
Thematic analysis → pain points → tasks → design requirements
Do users start from code?  •  Do they lose context across distant cells?  •  Does a visit history support real resumption tasks?  •  What evidence makes an automatic link trustworthy?

InterLink used semi-structured interviews with six experienced shared-notebook users. Participants inspected a notebook for up to 20 minutes and discussed challenges and desired features. This proposal adds critical-incident and resumption probes targeted to LinkMaker. Source: https://arxiv.org/html/2502.16114
Does output-aware context improve the correctness and coverage of inferred relationships?
H1: output text + generating code increases relation F1 over code-only context.
Do inspectable links improve notebook understanding?
H2: LinkMaker improves accuracy and inverse efficiency over standard Jupyter.
Does semantic history help readers return to prior evidence?
H3: history reduces revisit time, scrolling and navigation steps.
Do reasons and exact evidence help users verify suggestions?
H4: explanations improve calibrated acceptance and error detection.
These hypotheses map each proposed function to a measurable outcome. Results may reject any feature; that is preferable to positioning an unvalidated feature as the contribution.
Two or more annotators label cell pairs, exact spans and output regions. Resolve disagreements and report agreement.
Code only vs + output text; chart/output alone vs + generating code; full context vs retrieved candidates.
Cell-link precision, recall and F1; span overlap/IoU; output-region IoU; token cost, latency and failure rate.
Report improvement with confidence intervals and error categories—not only a single model run or anecdotal examples.

InterLink's evaluation relationships were manually annotated and refined, which provides a useful precedent for ground-truth creation. LinkMaker must additionally evaluate automatic inference. Source: https://arxiv.org/html/2502.16114
Controlled user study for the interface
Within-subject, counterbalanced study. Primary baseline: standard Jupyter. Secondary ablation: LinkMaker without semantic history.
Find a fact; explain code behavior; integrate Markdown, code and output; verify a suggested link; resume after interruption.
Target practicing data scientists. Use notebooks and domains matched for difficulty; pilot the task set first.

InterLink used a within-subject design with 12 participants, two notebooks, counterbalancing, task accuracy, confidence, completion time, inverse efficiency, SUS/Likert ratings and qualitative feedback. It reported a 13.6% accuracy improvement. Source: https://arxiv.org/abs/2502.16114
Validate users, tasks and pain points
Create expert ground truth and agreement rules
Test output context, generating code and retrieval
Repair tasks, timing and interaction issues
LinkMaker supports evidence-aware comprehension by automatically creating, explaining and revisiting relationships in computational notebooks.

Recommended next artifacts: interview guide, consent/recruitment plan, annotation handbook, frozen notebook benchmark, analysis plan and pilot protocol. Related sources: InterLink https://arxiv.org/abs/2502.16114 ; Themisto https://arxiv.org/abs/2102.12592 ; Voder https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/research/publication/augmenting-visualizations-with-interactive-data-facts-to-facilitate-interpretation-and-communication/ ; Shneiderman https://hci.stanford.edu/courses/cs448b/papers/shneiderman96eyes.pdf
